question: Why might a standard health pamphlet fail if you just hand it out to any community without checking?

options.A: Only medical doctors are legally allowed to read pamphlets
options.B: Pamphlets are universally banned by the ministry of health
options.C: It may ignore the unique setting, culture, and lifestyle of the group
options.D: Printed paper cannot carry any medically accurate information

explanation: Brilliant insight! One size doesn't fit all in nursing. Care must always fit the specific culture and lifestyle of the people we serve.

question: Which compress is best for a patient who twisted their ankle just ten minutes ago?

options.A: Alternating hot and steaming compress
options.B: Room-temperature dry wrap
options.C: Cold compress
options.D: Warm compress

explanation: For fresh injuries (acute injuries), cold therapy is your best friend to keep swelling and pain down.

question: Which factor is most important when deciding if a medicine belongs on an essential drug list?

options.A: How recently the drug was invented in a laboratory
options.B: National disease prevalence and public health needs
options.C: The marketing budget of the manufacturing company
options.D: Whether the drug is packaged in a colorful container

explanation: Exactly! We pick drugs based on the actual illnesses that trouble our local communities the most.

question: How do blood-borne pathogens usually spread during unsafe injection practices?

options.A: Consuming food prepared by an infected healthcare worker
options.B: Skin-to-skin contact between nurse and patient
options.C: Inhalation of dried viral particles in hospital air vents
options.D: Direct inoculation of contaminated blood into body tissues

explanation: Unsafe needles bypass our body's defenses and deposit infected blood straight into subcutaneous, intramuscular, or intravenous spaces. Makes total sense when you picture it!

question: Why do many pregnant women complain of lower back pain and wobbly joints?

options.A: Excess weight causes rapid cartilage breakdown in the knees
options.B: Relaxin softens ligaments all over the body, not just the pelvis
options.C: The growing fetus puts direct pressure on the spinal vertebrae
options.D: Calcium is actively pulled out of the joints to build fetal bones

explanation: You nailed it. Because relaxin circulates everywhere, joints all over the body become looser, meaning supporting muscles have to work extra hard (hello, backache!).

question: Why do certain medications need to be taken strictly on an empty stomach?

options.A: To ensure the liver enzymes are completely deactivated during digestion
options.B: To speed up the digestive process in the large intestine
options.C: To increase the overall acidity of the liver portal system
options.D: To prevent food from binding to the drug or delaying its absorption

explanation: Some foods love to mess with medications by chemically binding to them or slowing down how fast the stomach empties, which changes how much medicine actually gets into the blood.

question: Which behavior from a nurse will immediately make a teenager shut down and stop talking?

options.A: Listening actively to the patient's concerns
options.B: Maintaining a calm and welcoming facial expression
options.C: Asking simple open-ended questions
options.D: Displaying a judgmental or scolding attitude

explanation: Spot on! Scolding or moralizing makes teens feel ashamed, leading them to hide important health information and avoid future visits.

question: As a bedside nurse, why are you considered right at the center of hospital waste management?

options.A: Nurses are the only staff members allowed to touch trash
options.B: Nurses are legally liable for the city waste trucks
options.C: Nurses generate waste during daily patient care activities
options.D: Hospital management forces nurses to pay for disposal bins

explanation: Spot on! Because we give direct patient care every day, we are the first ones to handle and discard medical materials.

question: Which of the following best describes continuous quality improvement in a nursing unit?

options.A: Making small, ongoing changes to solve identified problems and better patient care
options.B: Waiting for a major hospital disaster before updating any clinical rules
options.C: Keeping all nursing routines exactly the same for ten years
options.D: Punishing nurses whenever a patient complains about the food

explanation: You nailed it! Quality improvement is all about making steady, daily adjustments to our workflows to give our patients the best care possible.

question: When you gently feel (palpate) a mother's tummy to check her uterus after birth, what is your main goal?

options.A: To confirm that the uterus is firm and contracting
options.B: To check if the bladder is completely empty
options.C: To stimulate milk production in the breasts
options.D: To measure the exact weight of the mother

explanation: A nice, hard, contracted uterus (like a firm mango!) stops bleeding. If it feels soft or boggy, that's a red flag for postpartum hemorrhage.

question: What is the common medical name for the external female reproductive organs?

options.A: The vestibule
options.B: The vulva
options.C: The introitus
options.D: The perineum

explanation: You've got this! The entire external female genital area is known medically as the vulva. It's a handy term to remember for your clinical rotations.

question: Which of the following is NOT a common challenge faced by community health nurses?

options.A: Poor road infrastructure and difficult geographical terrain
options.B: Inadequate medical supplies at primary healthcare centers
options.C: Unlimited availability of advanced surgical equipment in every village
options.D: Resistance from traditional or cultural belief systems

explanation: Community clinics rarely have unlimited advanced surgical equipment; resource scarcity is actually a major challenge in community practice. [learn more](GNS225_U2_T26#GNS225_U2_T26_h8)

question: What is the main focus of 'pharmacovigilance'?

options.A: Transporting bulk cargo across regional borders
options.B: Monitoring and reporting adverse drug reactions
options.C: Setting international market prices for herbal supplements
options.D: Manufacturing sterile equipment for surgical theatres

explanation: Well done! Pharmacovigilance is just a fancy word for watching out for and reporting drug side effects to keep patients safe.

question: How can bedside nurses help lower overall health care costs?

options.A: By preventing hospital-acquired complications and minimizing supply waste
options.B: By charging patients directly for bedside nursing procedures
options.C: By eliminating all diagnostic tests from patient care plans
options.D: By shortening physician consultation times during emergencies

explanation: Stopping problems like pressure sores or infections keeps patients safe, out of intensive care, and saves money on wasted supplies.

question: What shape is the anterior fontanelle (the soft spot towards the front of a baby's head)?

options.A: Triangle
options.B: Square
options.C: Circle
options.D: Diamond

explanation: The anterior fontanelle is famously diamond-shaped. This is a classic midwife clue that helps you tell it apart from the triangular posterior fontanelle during an exam!

question: What equipment do you attach directly to an oxygen source to control how fast the gas flows?

options.A: Pressure gauge
options.B: Pulse oximeter
options.C: Flow meter
options.D: Humidifier bottle

explanation: The flow meter is your best friend for control—it lets you accurately dial in the exact liters per minute prescribed for your patient.

question: A nurse held two town hall meetings and shared 500 flyers about clean water. To see if the advocacy actually worked (the outcome), what should the nurse check next?

options.A: How many total hours the nurse spent walking to the meeting venues
options.B: How boxes of leaflets were left over in the clinic storage room
options.C: Whether the printer charged a fair market price for the paper used
options.D: Whether the local government committed funds to fix the water source

explanation: You've got it! Handing out flyers is just the activity; seeing if the government actually takes action tells you if your advocacy made a real-world difference.

question: In the famous 'CAUTION' warning signs of cancer, what does the letter 'U' stand for?

options.A: Unexplained weight gain
options.B: Urinary tract infection
options.C: Unusual bleeding or discharge
options.D: Ulceration of the skin

explanation: Remember CAUTION! The 'U' reminds us to never ignore unexplained bleeding or discharge from any part of the body. Keep that in your nursing toolkit!

question: Why might two people experience the exact same traumatic event, but only one develops PTSD?

options.A: They have different underlying vulnerabilities and coping resources
options.B: The person who stayed healthy must have taken secret vitamins
options.C: Psychological trauma only affects individuals with high blood pressure
options.D: Trauma never causes long-term mental health problems in adults

explanation: Individual differences in genetics, past experiences, and coping skills mean stress affects people differently based on the diathesis-stress model. [learn more](GNS314_U2_T4#GNS314_U2_T4_h6)

question: What is a major risk of keeping a urinary catheter in place without strict sterile technique?

options.A: Rapid weight gain and fluid retention
options.B: Instant muscle atrophy in the legs
options.C: Catheter-associated urinary tract infections
options.D: Severe high blood pressure spikes

explanation: You got it. Catheters give bacteria a free highway straight into the bladder, which is why sterile technique is non-negotiable!

question: What substance is commonly mixed with pharmaceutical waste during encapsulation to lock it away safely?

options.A: Cement mortar or bitumen
options.B: Dry river sand
options.C: Cooking vegetable oil
options.D: Pure liquid mercury

explanation: Encapsulation uses solidifying agents like cement to lock hazardous drugs into a solid block, keeping them from leaking into the environment.

question: Which of these actions with a used sharps box is dangerous and completely wrong?

options.A: Storing the closed box in a designated utility room
options.B: Labeling the box with the date it was sealed shut
options.C: Placing the box within arm's reach of the injection site
options.D: Shaking or emptying the box to reuse it for more waste

explanation: Never shake or try to empty a sharps box. That puts you and others at direct risk of needle injuries.

question: What does an "out-of-pocket" payment mean in healthcare?

options.A: Reimbursement given to nurses for buying personal uniforms
options.B: Grants donated by foreign organizations to rural clinics
options.C: Monthly salary deductions paid automatically by the government
options.D: Direct cash payment made by patients at the point of receiving service

explanation: Spot on! Out-of-pocket means the patient is dipping straight into their own wallet to pay for drugs, tests, and consultations right there at the hospital.

question: In many homes, unfair food sharing puts which group at the highest risk of poor nutrition?

options.A: Young children and pregnant or lactating women.
options.B: Older teenage boys who play sports.
options.C: Elderly grandparents who live independently.
options.D: Adult male wage earners who work outside the home.

explanation: You're right! Even though their bodies need extra nutrients for growth and health, these groups often end up with the smallest shares.

question: What does 'Prior Informed Consent (PIC)' require before hazardous waste can be exported?

options.A: Approval from international shipping insurance companies
options.B: A public vote in the exporting nation's capital city
options.C: Written approval from the importing and transit countries
options.D: Permission from the World Health Organization director

explanation: You're doing great! PIC means any country receiving the waste—plus any countries the cargo passes through—must give their official written permission first.

question: Where must the urine drainage bag be placed at all times?

options.A: Level with the patient's hips
options.B: Resting directly on the patient's chest
options.C: Hanging from the top of the bed frame
options.D: Below the level of the bladder

explanation: You got it! Gravity is our friend here. Keeping the bag lower than the bladder keeps urine flowing smoothly downward and stops dirty urine from washing back up.

question: Which group of worms are flat, ribbon-like, and segmented?

options.A: Trematodes
options.B: Cestodes
options.C: Protozoa
options.D: Nematodes

explanation: Great try! Cestodes are our tapeworms—easily recognized by their flat, segmented ribbon-like bodies.

question: What is the main difference between a harmless (benign) vulval growth and a cancerous (malignant) one?

options.A: The presence of local itching and mild discomfort
options.B: The total size of the lesion when first measured
options.C: The ability to invade nearby tissues and spread
options.D: The exact location on the labia majora or minora

explanation: Well done! Malignant growths are dangerous because they can invade surrounding tissues and spread to other parts of the body.

question: A nurse tells an assistant to check vital signs on a stable patient and report back immediately if anything changes. Which right of delegation is this?

options.A: Right institution
options.B: Right direction
options.C: Right equipment
options.D: Right finance

explanation: Giving clear, concise instructions and letting the person know exactly what to report is all about getting the 'right direction' step right.

question: Which of these is NOT a typical challenge faced by public health agencies in developing regions?

options.A: Poor infrastructure delaying medical supply distribution
options.B: Shortages of trained public health professionals
options.C: Excessive, unlimited financial funding and surplus resources
options.D: Insufficient funding and budget constraints

explanation: Correct! Health agencies sadly almost never have a surplus of cash; they usually struggle with underfunding and resource shortages.

question: How should the little prongs of a nasal cannula face when you put them into a patient's nose?

options.A: Flattened sideways
options.B: Pointing straight up
options.C: Curving downward
options.D: Tilted backward

explanation: They are shaped to match human anatomy! Pointing them downward ensures they slide comfortably along the natural curve of the nasal passages.

question: What is the best way to assess a toddler's neurological function during a physical exam?

options.A: Observe their spontaneous play and developmental milestones
options.B: Ask them to complete a written multiple-choice test
options.C: Keep them completely still and silent for thirty minutes
options.D: Perform a strict formal cranial nerve exam immediately

explanation: Toddlers cannot follow complex commands, so observing natural movement and play provides the best clinical insight. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T1#GNS221_U2_T1_h7)

question: Why must nurses check a patient's liver function before starting a long course of albendazole?

options.A: Healthy liver function prevents worms from entering the bloodstream
options.B: Liver cells store the medication for up to six months
options.C: Hepatic enzymes are needed to activate the drug in the stomach
options.D: The medication is metabolized primarily through the liver

explanation: Brilliant! Because the liver breaks down these drugs, we need to make sure it's healthy enough to handle the workload without causing toxicity.

question: Where in the skin are Langerhans cells mostly found?

options.A: The subcutaneous fat
options.B: The hypodermis
options.C: The sweat ducts
options.D: The epidermis

explanation: Spot on! They hang out right in the epidermis so they can easily catch any germs trying to sneak in from the outside. [learn more](GNS211_U2_T3#GNS211_U2_T3_h4)

question: What is a major challenge for proper waste management in clinics with limited resources?

options.A: Strict enforcement of international laws
options.B: Excessive funding and overstaffing
options.C: Shortages of proper segregation supplies and erratic electricity
options.D: Too many advanced incinerators

explanation: Lack of steady power and basic items like safety boxes can make sticking to textbook waste rules tough in everyday rural practice.

question: Which of these is NOT a sign or effect of Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS)?

options.A: Presence of multiple small ovarian cysts
options.B: Irregular or absent ovulation
options.C: Interference with normal follicular development
options.D: Continuous production of excess mature ova

explanation: PCOS actually makes normal ovulation harder, rather than flooding the body with extra healthy, mature eggs. You're mastering this!

question: When assessing a patient's chest pain, what should the nurse evaluate first?

options.A: The patient's current employment status and stress level
options.B: The cost of the prescribed medications at the pharmacy
options.C: The exact characteristics, timing, and triggers of the pain
options.D: The patient's family medical history from childhood

explanation: Evaluating the nature, onset, and triggers of chest discomfort helps determine if the heart muscle is experiencing acute ischemia. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T4#GNS213_U1_T4_h8)

question: You are planning a fun health talk on teenage reproductive health in a secondary school. What approach works best?

options.A: Flannel graphs depicting geriatric care management
options.B: Megaphone announcements in the central cattle market
options.C: Complex medical journals left in the staff room
options.D: Interactive drama or peer-led discussions

explanation: Teens connect best with lively, relatable methods like drama and chats with peers rather than reading boring medical documents.

question: Why is the fear of social rejection particularly dangerous for teenagers facing choices about sex?

options.A: It forces their bodies to produce excessive stress hormones instantly
options.B: It permanently damages their ability to form friendships as adults
options.C: It automatically leads to severe clinical depression
options.D: It can cause them to ignore their own safety and boundaries just to fit in with friends

explanation: Fitting in is a major priority during adolescence, and the fear of being mocked often pushes teens to engage in unprotected sex against their better judgment. [learn more](GNS312_U3_T9#GNS312_U3_T9_h4)

question: What is the most important environmental requirement when screening a patient for gender-based violence?

options.A: Absolute privacy away from family members and partners
options.B: Conducting the interview in a busy, open hospital hallway
options.C: The presence of at least three armed security guards
options.D: Having a video camera recording the entire conversation

explanation: Survivors cannot speak freely if the abuser or other family members are present to overhear the discussion. [learn more](GNS312_U4_T12#GNS312_U4_T12_h5)

question: What happens if you manage to disrupt just one single link in the chain of infection?

options.A: The pathogen automatically changes into a harmless virus
options.B: The susceptible host becomes permanently immune
options.C: The infection process is completely stopped
options.D: The reservoir doubles its reproductive rate

explanation: Brilliant! The chain needs every single link to stay connected. Break just one, and the disease is stopped in its tracks.

question: Why might a high fever temporarily lower a male patient's sperm count?

options.A: White blood cells consume all available nutrients inside the seminiferous tubules
options.B: Higher body temperature disrupts the cool environment needed for healthy sperm development
options.C: Infections directly destroy mature sperm cells stored inside the urinary bladder
options.D: Fever causes the pituitary gland to permanently stop producing testosterone

explanation: Remember, sperm love cooler temperatures! A high fever raises the temperature in the scrotum, which temporarily pauses or slows down normal sperm production.

question: What is the big advantage of using single-dose medication vials?

options.A: They let nurses reuse syringes safely
options.B: They make the medicine taste sweeter
options.C: They completely stop the risk of contaminating shared medicine bottles
options.D: They mean fewer patients will need shots

explanation: Single-dose vials are used once and thrown away. No sharing means no chance of passing germs into the next dose!

question: What is another common term used to describe a brand name drug?

options.A: Generic identifier
options.B: Chemical name
options.C: Universal formula
options.D: Proprietary name

explanation: A brand name is also called a proprietary name because the company 'properly' owns the rights to that specific marketing title.

question: What attitude should you always show when counseling a client who needs emergency contraception?

options.A: Skeptical and demanding proof
options.B: Non-judgmental and confidential
options.C: Public and sharing with family
options.D: Strictly moralizing and formal

explanation: As nurses, our job is to provide a safe, private, and judgment-free space so clients feel comfortable seeking help without fear of stigma. Excellent nursing values!

question: A mother brings in her baby who has had watery diarrhea for two days, looks very sleepy (lethargic), and has sunken eyes. What is your immediate nursing priority?

options.A: Measure the child's height and head circumference
options.B: Administer a routine measles vaccine immediately
options.C: Send the mother home with advice to wait another week
options.D: Assess hydration status and prepare for urgent medical referral

explanation: Spot on! Lethargy and sunken eyes mean severe dehydration, which can turn dangerous very quickly. They need urgent fluid care and a doctor's help right away.

question: Which of these is NOT a standard nursing responsibility during EENT exams?

options.A: Prescribing the specific antibiotic treatment plan independently
options.B: Setting up good lighting and positioning for the doctor
options.C: Watching out for any bad reactions to local numbing meds
options.D: Explaining the procedure to help the patient relax

explanation: Nurses prep patients, assist during the check, and keep things safe, but prescribing medications is outside the nursing scope of practice.

question: In a condition called hemothorax, what main substance builds up in the pleural space?

options.A: Serous fluid
options.B: Blood
options.C: Atmospheric air
options.D: Purulent pus

explanation: The name gives it a great clue—'hemo' always points to blood! You are doing fantastic learning these clinical terms.

question: Which task best shows a staff nurse directly participating in quality assurance?

options.A: Reporting a faulty intravenous pump before it harms a patient
options.B: Complaining about low salary during a shift handover
options.C: Refusing to help clean a patient after an accident
options.D: Leaving ward charts blank until the end of the week

explanation: Brilliant! Spotting a broken tool and speaking up before it hurts a patient is the textbook definition of proactive quality assurance in action.

question: What is the typical timeframe for a strategic healthcare plan?

options.A: One single shift
options.B: A single week
options.C: 3 to 5+ years
options.D: Exact minutes

explanation: Strategic plans look far into the future, usually spanning three to five years or more. [learn more](GST321_U1_T5#GST321_U1_T5_h3)

question: What is a common barrier that nurses frequently encounter in community mental health care?

options.A: Too many available hospital beds in rural areas
options.B: Chronic funding shortages and cultural stigma
options.C: An overwhelming surplus of trained psychiatrists
options.D: Excessive community demand for group therapy

explanation: Lack of financial resources and social stigma against mental illness are major obstacles to providing effective community care. [learn more](GNS314_U1_T7#GNS314_U1_T7_h8)

question: Why do courts hand down severe punishments, including imprisonment, for drug diversion in hospitals?

options.A: Because pharmaceutical companies demand strict punishment
options.B: Because doctors refuse to work with nurses who make errors
options.C: Because stolen drugs fuel illegal abuse and endanger public safety
options.D: Because hospitals lose a lot of daily operating revenue

explanation: Diverted prescription drugs often end up on the street, worsening community addiction and public health risks. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T13#GNS122_U1_T13_h8)

question: Which of these kitchen habits is actually a bad idea if you want to keep nutrients locked inside your food?

options.A: Discarding the water used to boil green vegetables
options.B: Steaming vegetables lightly instead of boiling them
options.C: Choosing whole or minimally refined grain options
options.D: Using leftover vegetable broth in preparing stews

explanation: Well spotted! Pouring away your boiling water washes away valuable vitamins. Try using that nutrient-rich water in your stews instead!

question: During a home visit to an 80-year-old client, what safety check should the nurse prioritize to prevent common injuries?

options.A: Removing all chairs from the house to encourage standing
options.B: Testing the patient's ability to run a half-marathon outdoors
options.C: Checking if the patient can drive a heavy transport vehicle
options.D: Inspecting floors for loose rugs and poor lighting to stop falls

explanation: Fall prevention is a critical part of geriatric care, and checking home hazards directly prevents injuries. [learn more](GNS324_U1_T8#GNS324_U1_T8_h4)

question: Which part of the brain is mainly responsible for keeping you awake and alert?

options.A: Corpus callosum
options.B: Suprachiasmatic nucleus
options.C: Ventrolateral preoptic nucleus
options.D: Reticular activating system

explanation: The reticular activating system acts like an internal alarm clock, sending steady wake-up signals to your brain. You've got this!

question: What tool should the nurse use to check if a warm poultice is safe to apply?

options.A: A heavy weight pressed onto the mixture
options.B: A metal needle poked into the patient's arm
options.C: Their own inner wrist or a thermometer
options.D: A bright flashlight held close to the paste

explanation: Testing the temperature on the sensitive inner wrist helps verify the poultice is warm, not burning hot. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T10#GNS221_U3_T10_h5)

question: What key visual finding does a clinician look for on the cervix during a speculum exam for acute cervicitis?

options.A: Pus-like discharge and tissue that bleeds easily
options.B: Complete closure of the internal cervical opening
options.C: Large fluid-filled cysts across the surface
options.D: Pale, dry, and glistening epithelial layers

explanation: During an exam, an angry, infected cervix often shows pus draining out and tissue that is fragile and bleeds at a touch.

question: When the Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System (RAAS) kicks in, what is its main job?

options.A: Increase blood volume and cause vasoconstriction
options.B: Decrease heart rate and promote fluid excretion
options.C: Stimulate direct potassium loss through the sweat glands
options.D: Dilate peripheral arteries and lower blood pressure

explanation: When blood pressure drops too low, RAAS comes to the rescue by tightening blood vessels and telling the kidneys to hold onto water and salt to boost pressure back up.

question: After a bronchodilator nebulizer treatment, a patient coughs heavily. What should the nurse encourage them to do next?

options.A: Swallow the mucus to keep the throat moist
options.B: Expectorate the loosened mucus into a tissue
options.C: Drink a large glass of ice-cold water immediately
options.D: Lie down flat on the bed to stop coughing

explanation: Coughing brings up the loosened secretions, so spitting them out into a tissue clears the airway safely. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T7#GNS212_U2_T7_h6)

question: What happens when a patient lacks essential haematinics?

options.A: Red blood cell production is impaired
options.B: White blood cells multiply uncontrollably
options.C: Platelets aggregate too quickly in vessels
options.D: The heart slows down its pumping rate

explanation: Without raw materials like iron, the bone marrow simply doesn't have what it needs to pump out enough red blood cells. Great job connecting the dots!

question: Why do clinics use the WHO staging system for HIV when lab tests for CD4 count are missing?

options.A: To guide clinical management using observable signs when CD4 counts are unavailable
options.B: To calculate the precise date when the patient was initially infected
options.C: To predict the exact genetic strain of the virus infecting the patient
options.D: To accurately measure the exact viral load circulating in the plasma

explanation: That's right! When lab equipment is scarce, checking physical signs and symptoms helps nurses and doctors choose the best care plan. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T2#GNS216_U6_T2_h5)

question: What is a common myth that scares young people away from hormonal contraception?

options.A: It automatically increases an individual's height by ten inches
options.B: It turns eye color into a completely different shade overnight
options.C: It causes permanent internal accumulation or organ rotting
options.D: It cures all forms of infectious diseases instantly

explanation: Baseless fears about pills piling up inside the body are common myths. Patient education clears this right up!

question: What does information asymmetry mean in the context of healthcare?

options.A: All treatment prices are publicly displayed online
options.B: Patients have equal access to medical textbooks
options.C: Providers know much more about medicine than patients
options.D: Governments hide medical research from the public

explanation: Information asymmetry describes the unequal knowledge gap between trained health professionals and everyday consumers. [learn more](GST322_U1_T4#GST322_U1_T4_h3)

question: When must a nurse researcher use non-parametric statistical tests?

options.A: When the research study is funded by a government hospital
options.B: When the data does not follow a normal bell curve distribution
options.C: When the sample size is extremely large and perfectly random
options.D: When all study variables are measured on a continuous scale

explanation: Brilliant! If your data is messy or skewed and doesn't fit that neat bell-shaped curve, non-parametric tests save the day.

question: A patient insists that their mother, who passed away years ago, is coming to visit today. What is the best nursing action?

options.A: Argue firmly that the mother is dead to teach them reality
options.B: Scold the family members for not correcting the patient's false memory
options.C: Ignore the comment completely and pretend you did not hear anything
options.D: Acknowledge the feeling behind the statement and gently redirect their attention

explanation: Argueing causes distress. Instead, validate their emotion ('You really miss your mum, don't you?') and gently steer their focus elsewhere.

question: What makes the Vagus nerve (Cranial Nerve X) stand out from most other cranial nerves?

options.A: It controls the sense of smell entirely on its own.
options.B: It has no sensory function whatsoever.
options.C: It travels all the way down into the chest and tummy.
options.D: It only activates during high stress or panic.

explanation: Fantastic! While most cranial nerves stay around the head, the vagus nerve wanders down to supply our chest and belly organs.

question: When a nurse asks a patient, 'What makes your stomach pain better or worse?', what are they checking?

options.A: Severity and duration
options.B: Quality and onset
options.C: Provoking and palliating factors
options.D: Region and radiation

explanation: Spot on! Asking what triggers or relieves the discomfort helps you figure out the provoking (starting) and palliating (soothing) factors.

question: A quality improvement nurse is reviewing patient falls over the past year. How can a histogram help?

options.A: By replacing all incident report paperwork with digital drawings
options.B: By proving which specific nurse was on duty during every single fall incident
options.C: By showing the frequency distribution of fall counts, revealing if high falls are common or rare
options.D: By listing the exact home phone numbers of patients who experienced a fall

explanation: Histograms show how often numbers happen, letting quality teams instantly see what's normal and what's an extreme outlier.

question: In stroke care, what does 'spasticity' mean?

options.A: Rapid wasting away of muscle tissue
options.B: Complete loss of all muscle sensation
options.C: Uncontrolled trembling during resting states
options.D: Involuntary muscle stiffness and tight spasms

explanation: Spot on! Spasticity is when muscles become tight and stiff because of nerve damage, making them hard to stretch out.

question: Which of these statements is actually FALSE regarding histograms and ogives?

options.A: A histogram is used exclusively for qualitative categories rather than numerical data
options.B: An ogive can be used to find medians visually whereas a histogram cannot do this easily
options.C: An ogive displays running cumulative totals while a histogram shows single group frequencies
options.D: A histogram uses bars while an ogive uses connected points to form a polygon

explanation: You nailed it! Both histograms and ogives are meant for numerical data—histograms use bars for separate groups, while ogives use connected points for running totals.

question: Why do traditional health clinics often make teenage patients feel unwelcome?

options.A: They only open during late night hours when teenagers are in school
options.B: They are required by law to report all visits to local police stations
options.C: They completely lack basic medical equipment for younger populations
options.D: They are usually structured and designed primarily for adults or young children

explanation: Standard clinics often overlook the specific developmental, social, and emotional needs of teenagers, making them feel out of place. You've got this!

question: Why do we need to check the expiration dates on AED electrode pads?

options.A: Old pads contain chemicals that become toxic when exposed to air.
options.B: The computer software will refuse to turn on if attached to expired pads.
options.C: Expired pads will automatically trigger a loud alarm that disrupts hospital wards.
options.D: The conductive gel on the pads can dry out over time, preventing proper shock delivery.

explanation: Over time, the sticky gel on the pads dries out. If the gel goes bad, the electricity won't pass through properly during a rescue.

question: A postoperative patient has a urine output of 15 mL over the last hour. What does this finding most likely suggest?

options.A: An infection in the urinary bladder
options.B: Overhydration causing the kidneys to shut down
options.C: Inadequate organ perfusion from low blood volume
options.D: A normal reaction to pain medication wearing off

explanation: When blood volume drops, the body reduces blood flow to the kidneys, causing urine production to fall well below normal levels. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T4#GNS123_U3_T4_h5)

question: What is a standard chest X-ray most commonly used to check for in the ward?

options.A: Viewing active blood flow inside brain tissue
options.B: Checking for pneumonia or heart enlargement
options.C: Measuring exact electrical heart rhythms
options.D: Detecting microscopic bacterial infections in blood

explanation: Chest X-rays give us a clear view of the lungs and heart size, making them perfect for spotting conditions like pneumonia.

question: Why is it a bad idea to go grocery shopping on an empty stomach?

options.A: It makes non-essential snacks and food items look more tempting
options.B: It slows down the speed at which cashiers process payments
options.C: It causes sudden low blood pressure in the store aisle
options.D: It prevents the buyer from finding the correct grocery store

explanation: So true! Shopping while hungry always makes everything look delicious, leading to costly impulse buys you didn't budget for.

question: What is the main reason we teach patients respiratory hygiene and cough etiquette?

options.A: Reducing the cost of cleaning medical equipment
options.B: Preventing foodborne illnesses among patients
options.C: Containing respiratory pathogens at the source
options.D: Purifying the air inside closed hospital wards

explanation: Spot on! Cough etiquette stops germs right where they start—catching them in a tissue or elbow before they can fly into the air.

question: In the Three Delays model, what does the 'first delay' stand for?

options.A: Delay in arriving at the hospital due to bad roads
options.B: Delay in receiving treatment from doctors
options.C: Delay in diagnosing the pregnancy
options.D: Delay in deciding to seek medical care

explanation: The first delay happens right at home or in the community—when family members take too long to recognize danger signs or hesitate to go to the hospital.

question: What should you do if a patient's room is too dark when you are trying to check their skin?

options.A: Ask the patient to turn on all the household television sets.
options.B: Use a portable examination light to properly view the skin.
options.C: Skip the skin inspection until the patient visits the clinic.
options.D: Rely entirely on touch and palpation to detect any skin rashes.

explanation: Correct! Good lighting is a must for spotting subtle rashes, bruises, or color changes that you'd miss in a dark room.

question: What particle size is generally needed for medication to reach the deep lower airways and alveoli?

options.A: Between 50 and 100 micrometers
options.B: Greater than 20 micrometers
options.C: Between 1 and 5 micrometers
options.D: Any visible dust particle size

explanation: Fine particles measuring 1 to 5 micrometers are small enough to bypass the upper airway and settle deep in the bronchioles and alveoli. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T5#GNS212_U2_T5_h2)

question: What critical allergy information must you check before giving any new drug?

options.A: Favorite foods and dietary preferences
options.B: Known drug allergies and past adverse reactions
options.C: Family history of seasonal pollen allergies
options.D: Reactions to household cleaning supplies

explanation: Always ask about past drug reactions! It's a quick question that protects your patient from severe allergic responses like anaphylaxis.

question: When should nutritional screening typically happen for a newly admitted hospital patient?

options.A: Right before the patient is discharged home
options.B: At the final weekly multidisciplinary meeting
options.C: Only after the patient requests a meal tray
options.D: Within twenty-four hours of admission

explanation: Early screening within the first day helps catch risks before the patient's condition deteriorates. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T001#GNS227_U5_T001_h4)

question: A patient scheduled for discharge is crying and upset after a new diagnosis. What should the nurse do?

options.A: Postpone detailed instructions until the patient's emotional readiness improves
options.B: Ask a family member to take over all future health responsibilities
options.C: Hand the patient a textbook and tell them to read it alone
options.D: Proceed quickly with the teaching so the patient leaves on time

explanation: Well reasoned! High emotions block learning. Comforting the patient and waiting until they are calmer is always the right clinical call.

question: What is the most important rule for writing the methodology section?

options.A: It must prove that the hypothesis was completely correct
options.B: It must contain enough detail for another researcher to repeat the study
options.C: It must focus heavily on the personal feelings of the participants
options.D: It must avoid mentioning any ethical approval processes

explanation: Good science can be repeated! If your steps are clear, another nurse researcher should be able to run the exact same study.

question: What directly causes barotrauma in a patient on a ventilator?

options.A: Lack of early physical therapy and leg movement
options.B: Inadequate hand hygiene by the nursing staff
options.C: Bacterial infection growing in the endotracheal tube
options.D: High airway pressure or excessive lung volume

explanation: Too much pressure or blowing the lungs up like an over-inflated balloon can pop delicate air sacs, causing air to leak where it shouldn't.

question: What is a primary benefit of school feeding programmes?

options.A: Improving student concentration and cognitive development
options.B: Increasing the school fees paid by parents
options.C: Replacing the role of parents in family budgeting
options.D: Eliminating the need for any teaching staff

explanation: Adequate nutrition provides the energy and nutrients required for active learning and brain development. [learn more](GNS225_U4_T3#GNS225_U4_T3_h5)

question: How do the kidneys compare to the lungs in managing body pH?

options.A: Kidneys respond instantly to changes like the lungs do
options.B: Kidneys take longer to respond but have a higher capacity
options.C: Kidneys only regulate volatile acids while lungs handle others
options.D: Kidneys have a much weaker effect on blood pH than the lungs

explanation: Think of the lungs as the quick responders, while the kidneys are the heavy lifters. Renal compensation takes a few days to fully kick in, but it handles tough acids and gives powerful long-term control over your body's pH!

question: Which of the following is NOT a standard infection control practice in the home?

options.A: Cleaning equipment according to manufacturer guidelines
options.B: Disposing of used needles in a puncture-proof container
options.C: Keeping clean medical supplies separate from household waste
options.D: Washing hands only once at the beginning of the nursing shift

explanation: Spot on! Hand hygiene must be done frequently before and after patient contact, not just once when you walk through the door. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T11#GNS324_U3_T11_h7)

question: Why are daily reviews of invasive lines and breathing tubes an important part of complication prevention?

options.A: Hospital insurance policies require equipment to be changed daily.
options.B: It gives the nursing staff less paperwork to complete at shift change.
options.C: Removing them as soon as they are no longer needed lowers infection risks.
options.D: Patients prefer to have new lines poked into them every morning.

explanation: Every day a tube or line stays inside the body gives bacteria more time to enter and cause a severe infection. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T4#GNS321_U2_T4_h5)

question: Which child is at a higher risk for maltreatment?

options.A: Participating in community sports leagues
options.B: Excelling academically in primary school
options.C: Being the oldest child in a large family
options.D: Having a physical or developmental disability

explanation: Special needs require extra care, which can sometimes overwhelm stressed caregivers and increase vulnerability.
